title: Question 11
stem: Electrons are accelerated through a potential difference of $100\text{ kV}$. They are then incident on a metal target, they decelerate, and X-ray photons are emitted.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the maximum possible frequency of the emitted X-ray photons.
hints: Hint 1: Think about energy conservation - what is the maximum kinetic energy an electron gains from the 100 kV supply, and what happens if all of that energy becomes one single X-ray photon?
Hint 2: Convert the electron energy in eV to joules using $eV$, then equate it to $hf$ and rearrange for $f$ using $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$.
parts.proper_answer: Maximum photon energy $E_{max} = eV = hf_{max}$, so $f_{max} = eV/h = 2.4 \times 10^{19} \text{ Hz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link accelerating voltage to maximum photon energy**
Think of each electron as being given energy by the electric field. An electron of charge $e$ accelerated through p.d. $V$ gains kinetic energy $E_k = eV$. When it hits the target and decelerates, that energy can turn into an X-ray photon of energy $E = hf$. The maximum frequency happens when ALL the kinetic energy becomes ONE photon.

Step 2: **Calculate the frequency**
Equate the two energies: $$eV = hf_{max}$$ $$f_{max} = \frac{eV}{h}$$ Put in $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, $V = 100 \text{ kV} = 1.00 \times 10^{5} \text{ V}$, $h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s}$: $$f_{max} = \frac{(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(1.00 \times 10^{5})}{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}$$ $$f_{max} = 2.4 \times 10^{19} \text{ Hz}$$ This is the cut-off frequency. No photon can have higher frequency because no electron has more energy than $eV$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain why an aluminium filter may be placed in the X-ray beam when producing an X-ray image of a patient.

markscheme_points.text: Any 2 from: X-ray beam contains many wavelengths; so low energy X-rays are not absorbed in the; low energy X-rays can can cause harm but d

hints: Hint 1: Recall that the X-ray tube does not produce only one frequency - what range of photon energies is present in the beam hitting the patient?
Hint 2: Think about which photons are stopped easily by soft tissue - do low energy photons get through to the detector to help form the image, or are they just absorbed by the skin?
Hint 3: Connect filtering to patient safety and image contrast - why is it good to remove photons that do not contribute to the image?
parts.proper_answer: The beam contains a spectrum of energies. The aluminium filter absorbs most low-energy (soft) X-rays. These would otherwise be absorbed by tissue without reaching the detector, so they increase patient dose and harm without improving the image.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Remember the beam is a spectrum**
Decelerating electrons produce photons of many different energies up to the maximum from part (a). So the beam contains hard high-energy X-rays and soft low-energy X-rays.

Step 2: **See what soft X-rays do in the body**
Low-energy photons are easily absorbed in surface tissue. They do not have enough energy to pass through the patient to the film or detector, so they cannot contribute useful information to the image.

Step 3: **Explain the benefit of the filter**
The aluminium absorbs most of these low-energy photons before they reach the patient. This reduces the absorbed dose and risk of harm to the patient, while the remaining high-energy beam still gives good contrast for imaging. In short, filter hardens the beam.

parts.label: (c)
parts.part_stem:
The linear attenuation (absorption) coefficients $\mu$ for X-rays in bone, blood and muscle are given in Table 11.1.

Table 11.1

|  | $\mu / \text{cm}^{-1}$ |
| --- | --- |
| bone | 3.0 |
| blood | 0.23 |
| muscle | 0.22 |

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.text:
A beam of these X-rays is incident on a person.

Calculate the percentage of the intensity of the X-ray beam that has been absorbed after passing through $0.80\text{ cm}$ of blood.
hints: Hint 1: Focus on how X-ray intensity falls with thickness - which law links transmitted intensity $I$, initial intensity $I_0$, attenuation coefficient $\mu$ and thickness $x$?
Hint 2: Remember you are asked for percentage absorbed, not percentage transmitted - how will you convert the transmitted fraction into absorbed percentage?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply the attenuation law**
X-rays are absorbed exponentially: $$I = I_0 e^{-\mu x}$$ For blood, $\mu = 0.23 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ and $x = 0.80 \text{ cm}$. The transmitted fraction is: $$\frac{I}{I_0} = e^{-\mu x} = e^{-(0.23)(0.80)}$$ $$\frac{I}{I_0} = e^{-0.184} \approx 0.83$$ So about 83% gets through.

Step 2: **Find percentage absorbed**
Absorbed means not transmitted: $$\text{fraction absorbed} = 1 - \frac{I}{I_0} = 1 - 0.83 = 0.17$$ $$\text{percentage absorbed} = 0.17 \times 100\% = 17\%$$ A common slip is to give 83% as the answer - that is the transmitted part, always subtract from 100%.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text:
In an X-ray image, white regions show greater absorption of X-rays than dark regions.

State and explain the difference between the X-ray image of bone compared to that of muscle.

markscheme_points.text: bone is seen as lighter / muscle is seen as darker
either bone has a higher μ value so absorbs more or muscle has a lower μ value so transmits mor

hints: Hint 1: Look at Table 11.1 - how does $\mu$ for bone compare with $\mu$ for muscle, and what does a larger $\mu$ mean for absorption?
Hint 2: Use the rule given that white means greater absorption - which tissue will block more X-rays from reaching the detector and so appear whiter?
parts.proper_answer: Bone appears white (lighter) and muscle appears dark (darker). Bone has much larger $\mu$ ($3.0 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ vs $0.22 \text{ cm}^{-1}$) so absorbs far more X-rays and transmits far fewer to the detector.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Compare attenuation coefficients**
From the table, $\mu_{bone} = 3.0 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is more than ten times $\mu_{muscle} = 0.22 \text{ cm}^{-1}$. Larger $\mu$ means intensity falls much faster, so bone absorbs strongly while muscle transmits most of the beam.

Step 2: **Link to image brightness**
White regions show greater absorption. Because bone stops the X-rays, few reach the detector behind the bone, and that region is recorded as white or light. Muscle lets most X-rays through, so the detector receives high intensity and that region appears dark. This difference in $\mu$ gives the contrast that lets us see bone clearly.
